sources.news_title: USA Suing Former Venezuelan President Maduro for Torture
sources.text:
Venezuelas Ex-Präsident USA klagen Maduro wegen Folter an
Im Juni kommenden Jahres soll der Prozess gegen Venezuelas ehemaligen Staatschef Maduro in den USA beginnen. Er und seine Frau müssen sich dabei neuen Vorwürfen stellen - neben "Drogenterrorismus" ist nun auch von Folter die Rede.
Die USA haben den früheren venezolanischen Staatspräsidenten Nicolás Maduro wegen weiterer mutmaßlicher Verbrechen angeklagt. Neben "Drogenterrorismus" wirft ihm die Justiz laut einer geänderten Anklageschrift nun auch Folter von in Venezuela festgehaltenen US-Bürgern vor.
Maduro habe den Einsatz von Folter gegen bestimmte Personen genehmigt und ein System überwacht, das Folter, willkürliche Inhaftierungen und Gewalt als Mittel der Unterdrückung der politischen Opposition eingesetzt haben soll, heißt es in der Anklageschrift.
Physische und psychologische Folter?
Der ehemalige Staatschef und seine Frau sollen "vermeintliche Gegner durch Verfolgung und Gewalt terrorisiert haben", um an der Macht zu bleiben. Im Zeitraum von 1999 bis 2025 habe das Ehepaar Regierungsangestellte angewiesen, Mitglieder der Opposition durch schwere körperliche und psychische Schmerzen zum Schweigen zu bringen.
In der erweiterten Anklageschrift heißt es, ein Regierungsangestellter habe Foltermethoden entwickelt, die er sich von Maduro persönlich absegnen ließ. Ein weiterer Regierungsangestellter soll im Auftrag Maduros Oppositionellen mit Folter gedroht haben. Und ein dritter Regierungsangestellter soll an der Folterung von Regimegegnern durch Stromschläge beteiligt gewesen sein.
Seit Januar in US-Gefängnis
Maduro hatte Venezuela an der Spitze einer sozialistischen Regierung von 2013 bis 2026 autoritär geführt. Im Januar wurden er und seine Frau Cilia Flores in der venezolanischen Hauptstadt Caracas in einer umstrittenen Aktion von US-Spezialkräften gefangen genommen. Kritiker bezeichneten das Vorgehen als Verstoß gegen das Völkerrecht.
Der Vorwurf der USA lautete, der 63-Jährige habe sein Amt als Präsident und vorangegangene Posten in der Regierung über Jahre dazu genutzt, den Schmuggel von Tausenden Tonnen Kokain in die USA zu ermöglichen. Zudem soll er Diplomatenpässe an Drogenhändler verkauft, diplomatisch getarnte Flüge für Drogengelder ermöglicht und Drogentransporte geschützt haben.
Antrag von Ehefrau abgelehnt
Sowohl Maduro als auch seine Frau bestritten die Vorwürfe. Beide befinden sich seit Januar in einem Gefängnis in den USA. Im Juni 2027 soll der Prozess gegen sie beginnen. Im Fall eines Schuldspruchs droht dem Ehepaar allein für die neue Anklage wegen Folter eine Mindeststrafe von 50 Jahren im Gefängnis.
Sollten auch die bisherigen Anklagepunkte Drogenterrorismus und Kokainschmuggel zutreffen, muss das Ehepaar mit einer lebenslangen Haftstrafe rechnen. Den Antrag von Maduros Ehefrau, wegen gesundheitlicher Probleme das Gefängnis gegen Kaution zu verlassen, lehnte das Bundesgericht ab.
Mit Informationen von Martin Ganslmeier, ARD-Studio New York

sources.news_title: Maduro, wife face new torture charges. Here's what it means for their case
sources.text:
The criminal case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and former first lady Cilia Flores expanded Thursday dramatically after U.S. prosecutors unveiled new torture-related charges that they say are tied to a decades-long effort to maintain power through violence, intimidation and repression.
The superseding indictment adds a conspiracy-to-commit-torture count to an existing prosecution that already included narcoterrorism, cocaine-trafficking and weapons allegations. Prosecutors contend the couple used state institutions, security forces and allied groups to target opponents and detainees. The Justice Department alleges that multiple U.S. citizens were among the victims.
The move raises a broader question: Does the new charge materially change the government's case, or simply add another layer to a prosecution that was already poised to become one of the most consequential international criminal trials in recent U.S. history?
Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, were captured by U.S. forces at their Caracas home on January 3 and brought to New York to face federal drug-trafficking charges. Both have pleaded not guilty and are being held in federal custody while awaiting a trial currently scheduled for June 2027. The operation ended Maduro's 13-year rule of Venezuela, which is now led by his former vice president, Delcy Rodríguez.
Maduro attorney Barry Pollack responded to Newsweek's request for comment on Thursday, stating, “President Maduro denies the charges in the new indictment and looks forward to his day in court.”
DOJ Says Investigation Uncovered Additional Crimes
In a Justice Department statement shared with Newsweek on Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said investigators had continued working after the couple's arrest to uncover "the extent of their alleged crimes against the people of Venezuela and of the United States."
Blanche said the new charges are intended to bring "justice for the victims of torture, narcoterrorism, and organized crime."
The Justice Department alleged that for more than two decades, Maduro, Flores and members of their inner circle enriched themselves through corruption while suppressing opponents through "violence, threats, and physical torture under color of law." The department's statement said alleged victims included U.S. citizens and described conduct including electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, starvation, prolonged isolation and psychological torture. The DOJ statement stressed that an indictment is merely an allegation and that all defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.
In a statement accompanying the filing, Jamie McDonald, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, said the new indictment alleges that the couple and other leaders "conspired to repress dissent through grave violations of human rights" and that the alleged conduct included the torture of multiple Americans. The department also said the torture allegations are in addition to existing narcoterrorism, cocaine-importation and weapons charges carrying potential life sentences.
Legal Experts Say the Charges Could Strengthen the Prosecution
For prosecutors, the new count may do more than increase potential punishment.
David Weinstein, a former federal prosecutor and partner at Jones Walker, told Newsweek on Thursday the added allegations strengthen the case because they expand the overall picture prosecutors can present to jurors.
"It does strengthen the government's overall case against Maduro, to the extent that these additional allegations, tied to the conduct in the original indictment, furthers the overall heinous nature of the charges," Weinstein said.
The practical impact could emerge long before trial.
"The next step will be to see if this will cause the current trial setting to be extended/continued," Weinstein said. "I suspect that it will, since these additional charges will take more time to prepare to defend."
He also said defense attorneys could seek to separate the torture allegations from the existing narcotics case through a motion to sever the counts.
International Law Questions Could Become More Important
The new allegations also place the case within a broader international-law framework.
John Cerone, an international law scholar, said both the United States and Venezuela are parties to the Convention Against Torture, which requires countries either to prosecute alleged torturers or extradite them to jurisdictions willing to do so.
"From an international law perspective, it is significant that the U.S. is fulfilling its treaty obligation by prosecuting these individuals," Cerone told Newsweek on Thursday.
Cerone said the case could test the limits of head-of-state immunity, a principle that traditionally shields sitting leaders from foreign courts.
He pointed to the landmark case involving former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet in the United Kingdom, where courts found that former heads of state could face prosecution abroad under the Torture Convention even when the alleged conduct occurred while they were in office.
Cerone said the case is unusual because torture charges can trigger a form of universal jurisdiction.
According to Cerone, the new prosecution could ultimately influence accountability efforts beyond the United States because evidence gathered by American investigators may later prove valuable elsewhere.
"The U.S. prosecution could bring to light additional, and perhaps more robust, evidence that could then be used by these bodies, as well as by foreign courts," he said.
What Happens Next
The immediate question is whether the new charge affects the path to trial.
Weinstein said defense attorneys could seek additional time to prepare their case and may attempt to sever the torture count from the existing narcotics prosecution.
Beyond the courtroom, Cerone said observers should watch how foreign governments and international legal bodies respond.
"It will be interesting to see the attitude of other governments toward this prosecution," he said, including whether they view it as enforcement of international anti-torture obligations or a politically motivated proceeding.
Cerone also said future legal disputes could involve claims of head-of-state immunity and other international-law questions stemming from Maduro's former position in Venezuela.
Whether prosecutors can prove the allegations remains for a jury to decide. But legal experts told Newsweek that the new allegations have transformed the case from a major narcotics prosecution into a broader effort to hold a former head of state accountable for alleged human-rights abuses.

The Justice Department on Thursday announced new charges against former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores.
“Venezuelan President NICOLÁS MADURO MOROS and former First Lady of Venezuela CILIA ADELA FLORES DE MADURO have been charged in a Superseding Indictment unsealed today with conspiring to commit torture, narcoterrorism, cocaine importation conspiracy, and weapons offenses,” the Justice Department stated.
“As alleged in today’s Superseding Indictment, for more than two decades, Nicolás Maduro Moros and Cilia Adela Flores De Maduro engaged in a conspiracy to commit torture, including the torture of United States citizens, in addition to the narcotics trafficking and weapons offenses already charged,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald.
“As described in the Superseding Indictment, the Maduros and other Venezuelan leaders abused their positions of trust to enrich themselves through narco-terrorism, cocaine trafficking, and other corruption, including by employing Venezuelan military, law enforcement, and other government entities under their control to flood the United States with illegal narcotics. Today’s indictment further alleges that the Maduros and other Venezuelan leaders conspired to repress dissent through grave violations of human rights by ordering and allowing violence, threats, and physical torture under color of law. As alleged, this included the torture of multiple United States citizens, who were subjected to unspeakable abuse. Today’s charges exemplify the tirelessness that we and our law enforcement partners will undertake to vindicate victims of crime, particularly American victims subjected to horrific treatment abroad,” McDonald continued.
“This case is the result of incredible cooperation among law enforcement agencies, and it shows that we and our law enforcement partners will make exceptional efforts to investigate and prosecute human rights abuses, narco-terrorism, and narcotics trafficking around the world,” McDonald said at a press conference.

sources.news_title: Maduro Faces New Charge of Torture of Venezuelans and Americans
sources.text:
The government has accused former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife of personally approving the torture of political prisoners — including Americans — as part of a conspiracy to punish political opposition, silence dissent and preserve their political power.
An updated indictment unsealed Thursday with a charge of conspiracy to commit torture sharply raises the stakes in the ongoing prosecution in Manhattan federal court of Maduro, who already faced multiple offenses including conspiracy to commit narco-terrorism and conspiracy to import cocaine.
Prosecutors, over 10 of the indictment’s 30 pages, described how Maduro employed his vast network of resources — including the feared General Directorate of Military Counterintelligence, the DGCIM, and the leftist narco paramilitary Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, the FARC.
Prosecutors say his jailed co-defendant and wife, Cilia Adela Flores de Maduro, a former high-ranking government official, also took part, once approving the kidnapping and torture of a half dozen soldiers in an attempt to root out dissention among the military ranks.
Trending
The indictment details the experiences of nine unnamed victims who were arrested in relation to efforts to quell protests or other political issues and then beaten, given electric shocks, deprived of food and water. It describes how Maduro would “decide, on a case-by-case basis, whether an individual who had been abused would be released or subjected to criminal prosecution.”
If they refused to talk, he “would ask questions including, ‘What can we do to make them talk?’” — sometimes making “suggestions for particular torture techniques, saying ‘do not let them sleep,’ or ‘pour water on them,’ at times laughing after hearing about the abuse of prisoners,” the indictment says.
The indictment describes the experiences of one American prisoner who was taken to Boleíta Norte prison, where he was given electroshocks and guards injected him with a mysterious substance that gave him seizures — all while accusing him of being part of a grand American conspiracy to kill Maduro.
The indictment also tells the story of another unidentified American who was visiting his family in August 2023 when he was allegedly kidnapped by DGCIM, beaten so hard from behind that he required hospital treatment, and at one point had a pistol shoved into his mouth and told to “say goodbye to everyone he knew.”
Guards at Boleíta Norte prison later electrocuted his testicles — and told him the only reason he remained alive was for a future prisoner swap with the United States, the indictment says.
Many of the torture scenes described in the superseding indictment relate to Maduro’s desperate attempts to maintain political control in Venezuela during the years when his regime struggled to remain in power. That includes a 2017 constitutional crisis when the Maduro loyalists in the nation’s supreme court took over the country’s legislature and 2024 sham presidential election that was widely censured around the globe.
But it also describes the depths of the suffering experienced by the Venezuelan people, thousands of whom have fled to neighboring countries and the United States.
Prosecutors in one segment of the indictment describe what played out behind the scenes as Maduro’s regime tried to hunt down a law enforcement officer who “had become a famous opponent of the regime,” since he one time flew a stolen helicopter around Caracas and another time stole weapons from a military command station.
That matches the actions of Óscar Alberto Pérez, a state police investigator who briefly became a hero when he went rogue in 2017 by stealing a helicopter, dropping nonlethal stun grenades on the Supreme Tribunal of Justice building, and documented his acts of resistance on social media.
Prosecutors say in the indictment that one of the law enforcement officer’s friends was arrested on January 4, 2018, by government security forces in a futile attempt to locate the renegade cop. A high-ranking Venezuelan official was physically present when the man was tortured for days and had his testicles electrocuted while interrogators threatened to kill his child, the indictment says.
In another instance, prosecutors in the indictment say Maduro personally ordered the kidnapping and torture of a Venezuelan military officer who was under suspicion of meeting with a former Venezuelan government official who’d joined the political opposition.
The man was tortured by the DGCIM: forced to experience simulated drowning 30 times, beaten and subjected to live wire electrocutions 20 times — only to experience further torture when he was taken to a FARC camp in rural neighboring Colombia. Maduro allegedly viewed a video recording of the man’s forced false confession, the indictment says.
Prosecutors also alleged that in 2022 Maduro summoned several judges to his presidential palace to bribe them with a $1,000 monthly stipend to issue rulings favorable to his administration. But when one judge refused secret orders to yank opposition political opponents from appearing on electoral ballots, her family members were “arrested and tortured” by the DGCIM, the indictment says.
The indictment details how one family member was forced to drink latrine water, subjected to tear gas in their jail cell and subjected to extreme conditions inside a freezing room with blaring noise where bright lights were kept on at all times — until the judge finally relented.
Maduro and his wife, who were taken from their official home in Venezuela on Jan. 3, 2026, during an American military operation, previously pleaded not guilty of the narcotics charges and have questioned the U.S. government’s legal ability to abduct and criminally charge a foreign head of state.

sources.news_title: New US indictment charges Maduro with overseeing machine of repression, torture of Americans
sources.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. prosecutors unveiled sweeping new criminal charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro on Thursday, accusing him and his wife of heading a state-sponsored system of repression responsible for the beating, asphyxiation and electric shock treatment of scores of victims, including several Americans.
The torture charges add to pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader and his wife, Cilia Flores, who were seized from their Caracas home by the U.S. military in January to face drug trafficking charges in New York.
The updated indictment “alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the Manhattan courthouse where the case is being handled. “This is the epitome of corruption.”
Maduro, the indictment claims, suggested torture methods, sought and received updates on specific victims’ treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner’s child “as a form of psychological torture.” On occasion, he would even laugh after hearing about the abuse of prisoners, prosecutors allege.
Flores, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends.
A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer. Flores' attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations.
The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators for allegedly conspiring to flood the U.S. with cocaine. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.
Flores’ lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest due to medical concerns.
Alleged torture victims included US citizens
The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro's ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year.
At the time, Maduro, a former bus driver lacking his predecessor's military pedigree, was struggling to make inroads with the armed forces — historically the arbiter of political disputes in Venezuela — as the oil-dependent economy began spiraling out of control and government opponents took to the streets.
Fearing a barracks revolt, Maduro authorized Venezuela’s feared DGCIM military intelligence agency to use torture against military insiders and opponents he saw as threatening his grip on power, prosecutors allege.
While the indictment doesn’t name the alleged victims, the descriptions of the deaths and imprisonment match those of several high-profile Maduro opponents. They include Leopoldo López, who spent more than three years in prison for leading anti-government protests, and former Chávez Defense Minister Raúl Baduel, who died in custody in 2021. Also described is the shocking death of Fernando Albán, an opposition politician who died in a fall from the 10th floor of an intelligence agency building that a U.S. court later determined was a “murder for hire.”
Three American victims of torture were also described in the indictment.
One, who matches the description of Osman Khan, was detained entering Venezuela in early 2022 and subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.
Khan was released in October 2022 along with former U.S. Marine corporal Matthew Heath and six American oil executives in exchange for two nephews of Flores jailed in the U.S. on narcotics convictions. He and Heath later sued in U.S. courts under a federal anti-terrorism law and in May, won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture.
“It’s incredible to see a dictator in court,” Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. “The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations.”
Ex Venezuelan spy chief is a key cooperator
Torture is considered a grave crime under international law and can be prosecuted by any competent court regardless of the victims’ nationality, said Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University who for decades headed Human Rights Watch. Still, prosecution of foreign officials in the U.S. is exceedingly rare, having been attempted only a handful of times, including against the son of Liberian President Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad’s Syria.
“The problem here isn’t a lack of jurisdiction but rather selectivity of prosecution,” said Roth. “It is unlikely that Maduro tortured anyone on his own. The former Maduro officials whom the Trump administration has now co-opted as its new allies are likely as complicit in torture as he is.”

Rodríguez, as Maduro's vice president, for years oversaw key elements of Venezuela's security apparatus, including the domestic spy agency, responsible for arbitrary detentions and other human rights abuses.

Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an “extreme” flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed.

He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she’s already on medication for that.
Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.

sources.text:
Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro and his wife charged over torture allegations
The new US charge adds to the existing drug trafficking case against Venezuela’s former president and first lady.
Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were charged in the US state of New York with conspiring to commit torture in connection with allegations that they tortured political opponents to maintain their power.
The indictment, filed on Thursday in a Manhattan federal court, adds one count of conspiracy to commit torture to the drug trafficking charges the couple already faced.
It alleges that Maduro and Flores were part of a conspiracy that used torture and other abuses to repress and punish political opponents. Prosecutors say the conspiracy ran from at least 1999 through 2025 and involved Venezuelan military, intelligence and law enforcement officials.
The indictment details several cases of alleged torture. One detainee was allegedly subjected to electric shocks and asphyxiation after being arrested following a 2018 drone attack that the Venezuelan government said was an attempt to assassinate Maduro.
The alleged abuses also extended to United States citizens detained in Venezuela, three of whom were cited in the indictment. In one case, in January 2025, Venezuelan intelligence officers arrested an American citizen who was not their intended target and beat him repeatedly over two days, which caused permanent injury to his eye. He was reportedly released about a year later and was warned by Venezuelan officials not to disclose that the government had abused him.
Prosecutors allege that Maduro personally directed or was regularly briefed on the abuse of detainees. In one instance, the indictment says Maduro was told that a detained military officer remained defiant and responded by ordering officials to “squeeze them harder”. Prosecutors say he went so far as to suggest specific torture methods for unrelenting victims.
In other cases, prosecutors allege Maduro was told about beatings, electric shocks and simulated drowning and directed officials to apply additional “pressure”. According to the indictment, Flores was present at some of the meetings where detainees and their treatment were discussed.
“The indictment … alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable. The members of Maduro’s broad conspiracy were not just sitting behind a desk,” said federal prosecutor Jamie McDonald at a news conference. “These members of the conspiracy were holding the shovel. American citizens were tortured, and so were thousands of Venezuelans, we allege.”
Maduro and Flores pleaded not guilty to the drug charges and have been held at Brooklyn’s Metropolitan Detention Center since their capture. Their trial is scheduled for June 1, 2027.
The charges pile on an ongoing criminal case against Maduro and Flores. A superseding indictment accuses Maduro of working with cartel groups to move cocaine through Venezuela towards the US.
Maduro was abducted and imprisoned on January 3, after US President Donald Trump authorised a military raid in Caracas.

The new accusations relate to the alleged torture of US citizens who were being held in Venezuela while Maduro was in power.
The superseding indictment unsealed on Thursday accuses the former presidential couple of "entrenching themselves in power" by presiding "over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens".
According to the indictment, the torture included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture".

"All of this was done to ensure that Maduro and Flores retained their power," prosecutors said outside the courthouse on Thursday.
"This conduct, we allege, has caused significant harm to Americans, to US citizens", prosecutors said, calling it "the epitome of corruption".

The court document alleges that she did so in order to protect members of her family who were involved in illegal activities.
The allegations contained in the superseding indictment echo many of the accusations long made by prisoners who have been released from detention in Venezuela.
Javier Tarazona, the head of a human rights group in Venezuela, told BBC Mundo's Norberto Paredes earlier this year how he and his brother were held in a tiny punishment cell for 46 days after being arbitrarily arrested.

Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro charged with torture in new U.S. indictment
sources.text:
U.S. prosecutors unveiled sweeping new criminal charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro on Thursday, accusing him and his wife of heading a state-sponsored system of repression responsible for beating, asphyxiating and submitting scores of victims to electric shocks, including several Americans.
The torture charges add to pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader and his wife, Cilia Flores, who were seized from their Caracas home by the U.S. military in January to face drug trafficking charges in New York.
The updated indictment “alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the Manhattan courthouse where the case is being handled. “This is the epitome of corruption.”
Maduro denies the charges and “looks forward to his day in court,” lawyer Barry Pollack said. Flores’ attorney said he hadn’t yet had time to review the new allegations.
The indictment claims that Maduro suggested torture methods, sought and received updates on specific victims’ treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner’s child “as a form of psychological torture.” On occasion, he would even laugh after hearing about the abuse of prisoners, prosecutors allege.
Flores, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends.
Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.
He and his wife pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators for allegedly conspiring to flood the U.S. with cocaine. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
Flores’ lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest due to medical concerns.
Former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro’s U.S. trial proposed for June, 2027 start
The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro’s ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year.
At the time, Maduro, a former bus driver lacking his predecessor’s military pedigree, was struggling to make inroads with the armed forces – historically the arbiter of political disputes in Venezuela – as the oil-dependent economy began spiralling out of control and government opponents took to the streets.
Fearing a barracks revolt, Maduro authorized Venezuela’s feared DGCIM military intelligence agency to use torture against military insiders and opponents he saw as threatening his grip on power, prosecutors allege.
While the indictment doesn’t name the alleged victims, the descriptions of the deaths and imprisonment match those of several high-profile Maduro opponents. They include Leopoldo López, who spent more than three years in prison for leading anti-government protests, and former Chávez Defense Minister Raúl Baduel, who died in custody in 2021. Also described is the shocking death of Fernando Albán, an opposition politician whose fall from the 10th floor of an intelligence agency building was later determined by a U.S. court to be a “murder for hire.”
Three American victims of torture were also described in the indictment.
One, who matches the description of Osman Khan, was detained entering Venezuela in early 2022 and subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.
Khan was released in October 2022 along with former U.S. Marine corporal Matthew Heath and six American oil executives in exchange for two nephews of Flores jailed in the U.S. on narcotics convictions. He and Heath later sued in U.S. courts under a federal anti-terrorism law and in May, won a US$300-million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture.
“It’s incredible to see a dictator in court,” Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. “The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations.”
Torture is considered a grave crime under international law and can be prosecuted by any competent court regardless of the victims’ nationality, said Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University who for decades headed Human Rights Watch. Still, prosecution of foreign officials in the U.S. is exceedingly rare, having been attempted only a handful of times, including against the son of Liberian President Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad’s Syria.
“The problem here isn’t a lack of jurisdiction but rather selectivity of prosecution,” said Roth. “It is unlikely that Maduro tortured anyone on his own. The former Maduro officials whom the Trump administration has now co-opted as its new allies are likely as complicit in torture as he is.”
Venezuela’s government has so far been silent about the new accusations against Maduro, reflecting the challenges facing acting President Delcy Rodríguez as she strives to appease the security forces without alienating President Donald Trump, whose support she can’t lose.
Rodríguez, as Maduro’s vice president, for years oversaw key elements of Venezuela’s security apparatus, including the domestic spy agency, responsible for arbitrary detentions and other human rights abuses.
The revised indictment appears to rely partly on the testimony of one of Maduro’s co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. Known throughout Venezuela by his nickname El Pollo, the Chicken, Carvajal served as Chávez’s spymaster and head of the DGCIM for more than a decade.
Carvajal pleaded guilty last year to the drug trafficking charges in New York after being extradited from Spain. Since then, he has been meeting with prosecutors building the case against Maduro. In an open letter to Trump last year, Carvajal, who broke with Maduro years ago, said he wanted “to atone by telling the full truth so that the United States can protect itself from the dangers I witnessed for so many years.”
The new charges were unveiled as Maduro’s wife, Flores, was in court Thursday for a previously scheduled hearing over her request to be released so she can undergo medical treatment. Flores’ lawyers said the 69-year-old former first lady has lost 11 kilograms while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July and has been told that she might need heart surgery.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was “thrown against a wall or dresser” during her capture.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an “extreme” flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed.
U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores’ request, siding with prosecutors who said she is an “extreme” flight risk. He noted, among other things, that she’s unwilling to undergo catheterization in jail in order to determine the cause of her heart problems and the appropriate steps for treatment.
He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she’s already on medication for that.
Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.

Flores, a former legislator and attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends.
A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro’s lawyer. Flores’ attorney said he hadn’t yet had time to review the new allegations.
The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
They face potential sentences of life in prison if convicted.
Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.
Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid. Flores’ lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest.
Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.
Alleged torture victims included US citizens
The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela’s feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro’s co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York and has offered to testify against his former boss.

Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.
Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela.
Among those who sued is Matthew Heath, a former U.S. Marine corporal from Tennessee. He was arrested at a roadblock in Venezuela in 2020 and held in custody for more than two years.
In May, Heath and another former prisoner won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. The lawsuit, brought under a federal anti-terrorism law, included allegations of waterboarding, electrocution, threats of rape with a nightstick, administration of mind-altering medications and the repeated use of a cramped cell nicknamed “El Tigrito.”
“It’s incredible to see a dictator in court,” Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. “The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations.”
Former first lady denied release for medical treatment
Meanwhile, Flores’ lawyers argued that Flores, 69, has medical problems that cannot be treated effectively in jail. She has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July, has “lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath” and has been told that she might need heart surgery, the attorneys said.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was “thrown against a wall or dresser” during her capture.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an “extreme” flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed.
U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores’ request. He noted, among other things, that she’s unwilling to undergo catheterization in jail in order to determine the cause of her heart problems and the appropriate steps for treatment.
He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she’s already on medication for that.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a “surgical law enforcement operation.” Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
Goodman reported from Miami. Associated Press writers Larry Neumeister and Jennifer Peltz in New York contributed to this report.
